claim: Peptidoglycan (PG) is the essential and major component of bacterial cell envelopes.
source: It icomprises glycan chains and peptide stems, both containing unusual amino acids and sugars.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a fundamental property of bacterial cell envelopes.

claim: PG comprises glycan chains and peptide stems, both containing unusual amino acids and sugars.
source: It icomprises glycan chains and peptide stems, both containing unusual amino acids and sugars.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of peptidoglycan.

claim: The lack of automated tools for PG analysis has hampered the ability to perform high-throughput analyses.
source: The lack of automated tools has hampered the ability to perform high-throughput analyses and prevented the adoption of a standard methodology.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the field that the current work addresses.

claim: The lack of automated tools has prevented the adoption of a standard methodology for PG analysis.
source: The lack of automated tools has hampered the ability to perform high-throughput analyses and prevented the adoption of a standard methodology.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the lack of automated tools.

claim: PGFinder represents a powerful tool to quantify PG fragments and discover novel structural features.
source: We applied the PGFinder pipeline to analyse the muropeptides composition of Escherichia coli which has been extensively studied. We demonstrate that PGFinder can capture an unprecedented level of complexity of PG structure, highlighting the limitations of the search strategies reported so far.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the application to E. coli analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: The characterisation of bacterial cell walls started with the development of electron microscopy techniques.
source: The characterisation of bacterial cell walls started with the development of electron microscopy techniques (Mudd and Lackman, 1941), and it has ever since been the focus of countless studies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to historical work.

claim: Peptidoglycan confers cell shape and resistance to osmotic stress.
source: It confers cell shape and resistance to osmotic stress and represents an unmatched target for antibiotics (Mainardi et al., 2008; Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Peptidoglycan represents an unmatched target for antibiotics.
source: It confers cell shape and resistance to osmotic stress and represents an unmatched target for antibiotics (Mainardi et al., 2008; Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Beta-lactams and glycopeptides are some of the most widely used antibiotics to date.
source: Some of the most widely used antibiotics to date (beta-lactams and glycopeptides) inhibit the polymerisation of PG.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about antibiotic classes.

claim: Beta-lactams and glycopeptides inhibit the polymerisation of PG.
source: Some of the most widely used antibiotics to date (beta-lactams and glycopeptides) inhibit the polymerisation of PG.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of action of these antibiotics.

claim: PG composition was characterised soon after its discovery.
source: PG (murein; originally known as mucopeptide) is a giant, insoluble, bag-shaped molecule, and its composition was characterised soon after its discovery (Cummins and Harris, 1956; Rogers and Perkins, 1959; Weidel and Pelzer, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citations to early work on PG.

claim: PG is composed of glycan chains containing alternating N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) residues linked by β,1–4 bonds.
source: It is composed of glycan chains containing alternating N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) residues linked by β,1–4 bonds.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the chemical structure of PG.

claim: The lactyl group of MurNAc residues is substituted by pentapeptide stems which often has the L-Ala1-γ-D-Glu2-L-DAA3-D-Ala4-D-Ala5 sequence.
source: The lactyl group of MurNAc residues is substituted by pentapeptide stems which often has the L-Ala1-γ-D-Glu2-L-DAA3-D-Ala4-D-Ala5 sequence, where DAA is a diamino acid such as meso-diaminopimelic (mDAP) acid or L-lysine (Figure 1a; Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a, with citation support.

claim: Peptide stem composition and polymerisation can vary amongst bacterial species.
source: Peptide stem composition and polymerisation can vary amongst bacterial species (Schleifer and Kandler, 1972).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: PG building blocks produced in the cytoplasm are always the same.
source: Whilst PG building blocks produced in the cytoplasm are always the same, the final structure undergoes constant lysis and modification, a process referred to as 'remodelling'.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle of PG biosynthesis.

claim: The final PG structure undergoes constant lysis and modification, a process referred to as 'remodelling'.
source: Whilst PG building blocks produced in the cytoplasm are always the same, the final structure undergoes constant lysis and modification, a process referred to as 'remodelling'.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of PG remodelling.

claim: PG structural plasticity plays a critical role for adaption to environmental conditions during host-pathogen interaction.
source: PG structural plasticity plays a critical role for adaption to environmental conditions during host-pathogen interaction (Boneca et al., 2007; Juan et al., 2018) or to survive exposure to antibiotics (Mainardi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: PG structural plasticity plays a critical role to survive exposure to antibiotics.
source: PG structural plasticity plays a critical role for adaption to environmental conditions during host-pathogen interaction (Boneca et al., 2007; Juan et al., 2018) or to survive exposure to antibiotics (Mainardi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: PG material is straightforward to purify.
source: PG material is straightforward to purify, but the structural analysis of this molecule is challenging and remains a time-consuming and labour-intensive process.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the difficulty of structural analysis.

claim: The structural analysis of PG is challenging and remains a time-consuming and labour-intensive process.
source: PG material is straightforward to purify, but the structural analysis of this molecule is challenging and remains a time-consuming and labour-intensive process.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the field.

claim: A transformative step for the characterisation of disaccharide peptides has been the use of reversed-phase HPLC (rp-HPLC) and mass spectrometry (MS) towards the end of the 1990s.
source: A transformative step for the characterisation of disaccharide peptides has been the use of reversed-phase HPLC (rp-HPLC) and mass spectrometry (MS) towards the end of the 1990s (Garcia-Bustos et al., 1988; Glauner, 1988; Glauner et al., 1988; Martin et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated with citations to the relevant historical work.

claim: Combining muropeptides separation by rp-HPLC and MS characterisation has hinted at a more complex structure than previously reported.
source: Combining muropeptides separation by rp-HPLC and MS characterisation has hinted at a more complex structure than previously reported.
evidence: This is stated as an outcome of the combined technique.

claim: The experimental strategy to analyse PG structure has barely changed over the past 30 years.
source: The experimental strategy to analyse PG structure has barely changed over the past 30 years.
evidence: This is stated as a criticism of the field.

claim: The analysis of MS data for PG remains a black box.
source: Even though rp-HPLC-MS has been routinely used over the past decade, the analysis of MS data remains a black box.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the field.

claim: Except for a recent study describing the PG structure of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, no information is available in the literature about the strategy used to identify muropeptides in rp-HPLC-MS datasets.
source: Except for a recent study describing the PG structure of Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Anderson et al., 2020b), no information is available in the literature about the strategy used to identify muropeptides in rp-HPLC-MS datasets.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the literature.

claim: Shotgun proteomics tools can be used for the automated and unbiased analysis of PG structure.
source: We previously provided the proof of concept that shotgun proteomics tools can be used for the automated and unbiased analysis of PG structure (Bern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The analysis of Clostridioides difficile PG led to the identification of many muropeptides never reported before.
source: The analysis of Clostridioides (previously Clostridium) difficile PG led to the identification of many muropeptides never reported before.
evidence: This is stated as a result from previous work.

claim: PG analysis can be carried out with relatively high throughput using microgram amounts of material.
source: This work also demonstrated that PG analysis could be carried out with relatively high throughput, opening the possibility to analyse large numbers of samples (such as clinical or environmental isolates) using a minimal amount of material (typically microgram amounts).
evidence: This is stated as a capability demonstrated in previous work.

claim: PGFinder is a versatile and straightforward open-source software tool that allows automated identification of muropeptides based on the creation of dynamic databases.
source: PGFinder is a versatile and straightforward open-source software tool that allows automated identification of muropeptides based on the creation of dynamic databases.
evidence: This is a direct description of the software developed in this work.

claim: PGFinder can be used in conjunction with freely available MS data deconvolution software.
source: Finally, we provide evidence that PGFinder can be used in conjunction with freely available MS data deconvolution software, making PG analysis possible using entirely open-access tools.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the work and demonstrated with MaxQuant.

claim: A first search was carried out using a database made of reduced disaccharide peptides (monomers) and their theoretical monoisotopic masses.
source: A first search was carried out using a database made of reduced disaccharide peptides (monomers) and their theoretical monoisotopic masses.
evidence: This describes the first step of the PGFinder algorithm.

claim: MS data were deconvoluted using the Protein Metrics Byos software to generate a list of observed monoisotopic masses alongside other parameters including retention times and signal intensity.
source: MS data were deconvoluted using the Protein Metrics Byos software to generate a list of observed monoisotopic masses alongside other parameters including retention times and signal intensity.
evidence: This describes the data processing step before PGFinder analysis.

claim: Any observed mass within 10 ppm tolerance was considered as a match.
source: Any observed mass within 10 ppm tolerance was considered as a match and the corresponding inferred structure and theoretical mass were then added to a list of matched structures (Figure 2, library 1).
evidence: This describes the matching criteria used in PGFinder.

claim: The list of matched monomers was used to build another database in silico corresponding to dimers and trimers and their theoretical masses.
source: As a second step, we used the list of matched monomers to build another database in silico (Figure 2, database 2), corresponding to dimers and trimers and their theoretical masses.
evidence: This describes the second step of the PGFinder algorithm, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Two types of polymerisation events are included in the original PGFinder version depending on the type of crosslink either through peptide stems or glycan chains.
source: Two types of polymerisation events are included in the original PGFinder version depending on the type of crosslink either through peptide stems or glycan chains.
evidence: This describes a feature of the PGFinder algorithm.

claim: The final library contained only modified muropeptides corresponding to matched monomers, dimers, and trimers.
source: The final library contained only modified muropeptides corresponding to matched monomers, dimers, and trimers.
evidence: This describes the content of the final search library in PGFinder.

claim: The modifications accounted for include the presence of anhydro groups, deacetylated sugars, amidated amino acids, and modifications resulting from N-acetylglucosaminidase or amidase activities.
source: The modifications accounted for include the presence of anhydro groups, deacetylated sugars, amidated amino acids, and modifications resulting from N-acetylglucosaminidase or amidase activities (loss of GlcNAc and lack of peptide stems, respectively).
evidence: This describes the types of modifications searched by PGFinder.

claim: In-source decay products and Na+/K+ salt adducts were added to library 3.
source: In-source decay products (loss of GlcNAc) and Na+/K+ salt adducts were also added to library 3.
evidence: This describes additional features included in the PGFinder search.

claim: The intensities of in-source decay products and salt adducts were combined with that from parent ions when found within close retention time (a 0.5 min time window).
source: The intensities of in-source decay products and salt adducts were combined with that from parent ions when found within close retention time (a 0.5 min time window).
evidence: This describes the cleanup step in PGFinder processing.

claim: The output of PGFinder is a matched table written to a .csv format file containing all the inferred structures identified within the specified mass and retention time windows with an extracted-ion chromatogram (XIC) signal intensity for quantification.
source: The output of this final step is a matched table written to a .csv format file. It contained all the inferred structures identified within the specified mass and retention time windows with an extracted-ion chromatogram (XIC) signal intensity for quantification.
evidence: This describes the output format of PGFinder.

claim: UHPLC-MS/MS data were acquired for three independent PG samples (biological replicates) of E. coli.
source: UHPLC-MS/MS data were acquired for three independent PG samples (biological replicates; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for E. coli analysis.

claim: A first search was carried out using a minimal mass database made of 10 simple PG fragments including three glycan chains and seven monomers.
source: A first search was carried out using a minimal mass database made of 10 simple PG fragments including three glycan chains (di-, tetra-, and hexasaccharides) and seven monomers (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the initial search database for E. coli analysis.

claim: Depending on the dataset analysed, 41–48% of the total ion intensity was assigned to PG structures.
source: Depending on the dataset analysed, 41–48% of the total ion intensity was assigned to PG structures.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the E. coli analysis.

claim: Inferred structures were frequently found with multiple retention times, reflecting the existence of stereoisomers.
source: As anticipated, inferred structures were frequently found with multiple retention times, reflecting the existence of stereoisomers, with one species accounting for most of the intensity.
evidence: This is an observation from the E. coli data analysis.

claim: More than 97% of the most abundant monomer GM-AEJA was eluted at an average retention time of 10.04 ± 0.04 min.
source: For example, >97% of the most abundant monomer GM-AEJA was eluted at an average retention time of 10.04 ± 0.04 min.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the E. coli analysis.

claim: Sixty PG fragments were identified in E. coli.
source: Data consolidation revealed an unprecedented muropeptide composition complexity compared to recent LC-MS analyses of E. coli (Kühner et al., 2014; Table 1—source data 2). Sixty PG fragments were identified (Table 1): these included glycan chains lacking peptide stems (4.38%), monomers (63.14%), dimers (29.54%), and trimers (2.94%) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a key result from the E. coli analysis, shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: E. coli PG fragments included glycan chains lacking peptide stems (4.38%), monomers (63.14%), dimers (29.54%), and trimers (2.94%).
source: Sixty PG fragments were identified (Table 1): these included glycan chains lacking peptide stems (4.38%), monomers (63.14%), dimers (29.54%), and trimers (2.94%) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative breakdown of E. coli PG composition shown in Figure 3.

claim: The crosslinking index of E. coli PG is 15.69%.
source: Based on the abundance of multimeric PG fragments, we report a crosslinking index of 15.69%, which is slightly lower than the value previously reported of 23.1% (Glauner, 1988).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the E. coli data.

claim: The crosslinking index of 15.69% is slightly lower than the value previously reported of 23.1%.
source: Based on the abundance of multimeric PG fragments, we report a crosslinking index of 15.69%, which is slightly lower than the value previously reported of 23.1% (Glauner, 1988).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The automated and unbiased search revealed several muropeptides that were expected but never reported to date for E. coli.
source: The automated and unbiased search revealed several muropeptides that were expected but never reported to date for E. coli.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding of the E. coli analysis.

claim: E. coli PG contains PG fragments resulting from amidase activity (4.55%), found as 'denuded glycans' and modified variants or muropeptide stem with an extra disaccharide residue.
source: These included (i) PG fragments resulting from amidase activity (4.55%), found as 'denuded glycans' (disaccharides and tetrasaccharides) and modified variants or muropeptide stem with an extra disaccharide residue;
evidence: This is a specific finding from the E. coli analysis.

claim: E. coli PG contains low-abundance (0.23%) PG fragments containing deacetylated GlcNAc residues.
source: (ii) a low-abundance (0.23%) PG fragments containing deacetylated GlcNAc residues;
evidence: This is a specific finding from the E. coli analysis.

claim: E. coli PG contains PG fragments resulting from glucosaminidase activity (0.12%).
source: and (iii) PG fragments resulting from glucosaminidase activity (0.12%).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the E. coli analysis.

claim: Deacetylated muropeptides were not expected since no E. coli PG deacetylase has been identified in this organism to date.
source: Deacetylated muropeptides were not expected since no E. coli PG deacetylase has been identified in this organism to date.
evidence: This is stated as context for the unexpected finding.

claim: All the structures identified for the first time in E. coli (glycan chains, monomers containing deacetyl groups, and muropeptides lacking a GlcNAc residue) were confirmed by MS/MS analysis.
source: All the structures identified for the first time (glycan chains, monomers containing deacetyl groups, and muropeptides lacking a GlcNAc residue) were confirmed by MS/MS analysis (Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated as validation of the novel findings.

claim: The proportion of muropeptides with anhydroMurNAc groups identified (4.55%) was in line with previous studies, yielding an average chain length of 36.05.
source: The proportion of muropeptides with anhydroMurNAc groups identified (4.55%) was in line with previous studies, yielding an average chain length of 36.05.
evidence: This is a calculated result from the E. coli data.

claim: The average chain length of 36.05 is higher than an earlier study that reported a predominant chain length of 5–10 disaccharide units.
source: This value is higher than an earlier study that reported a predominant chain length of 5–10 disaccharide units (Harz et al., 1990), but agreed with recent work that reported long glycan chains in E. coli (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The average chain length of 36.05 agreed with recent work that reported long glycan chains in E. coli.
source: This value is higher than an earlier study that reported a predominant chain length of 5–10 disaccharide units (Harz et al., 1990), but agreed with recent work that reported long glycan chains in E. coli (Turner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with recent literature.

claim: The quantification of muropeptides across biological replicates was very consistent, with Pearson's correlation coefficients >0.96.
source: Overall, the quantification of muropeptides across biological replicates was very consistent, with Pearson's correlation coefficients >0.96 (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of reproducibility shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The most pronounced variations in quantification were observed with low-abundance muropeptides accounting for less than 1% of the species identified.
source: The most pronounced variations in quantification were observed with low-abundance muropeptides accounting for less than 1% of the species identified.
evidence: This is an observation about the variability in the data.

claim: A more complex search with a mass database made of glycan chains and all possible monomers containing di-, tri-, tetra-, and pentapeptide stems identified several monomers with tetra- and pentapeptide stems containing unusual amino acids.
source: We further explored the structural diversity of E. coli PG, performing a more complex search with a mass database made of glycan chains and all possible monomers containing di-, tri-, tetra-, and pentapeptide stems (Table 1—source data 4; 224 structures in total). Several monomers with tetra- and pentapeptide stems containing unusual amino acids were identified.
evidence: This describes an extended analysis of E. coli PG.

claim: Only four structures containing unusual amino acids could be confirmed by MS/MS analysis (GM-AEJF, -AEJN, AEJK, -AEJAK, and GM-AEJKD).
source: Only four structures could be confirmed by MS/MS analysis and corresponding multimers were retained (GM-AEJF, -AEJN, AEJK, -AEJAK, and GM-AEJKD).
evidence: This is a result from MS/MS validation.

claim: Muropeptides containing unusual amino acids accounted for ca. 7.5% of the 80 structures identified using a complex mass database.
source: Collectively, muropeptides containing unusual amino acids accounted for ca. 7.5% of the 80 structures identified (Table 1—source data 5) using a complex mass database.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the extended E. coli analysis.

claim: PG samples were digested by mutanolysin, and disaccharide peptides were beta-eliminated to generate lactyl-peptides for C. difficile analysis.
source: To illustrate the versatility of the software, PG samples were digested by mutanolysin, and disaccharide peptides were beta-eliminated to generate lactyl-peptides (Tipper, 2002) and analysed by UHPLC-MS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method for C. difficile.

claim: The high-resolution PG structure of C. difficile has been described based on the MS/MS analysis of muropeptides.
source: Since the high-resolution PG structure of C. difficile has been described based on the MS/MS analysis of muropeptides (Bern et al., 2017), we used data previously published to build a PG fragment database for a 'one-off' matching step.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: All monomers and dimers searched were identified in C. difficile, except for two muropeptides containing a peptide stem with a methionine residue in position four.
source: All monomers and dimers searched were identified, except for two muropeptides containing a peptide stem with a methionine residue in position four, both present in low abundance in C. difficile strain 630 (ca. 0.10%).
evidence: This is a result from the C. difficile analysis.

claim: 25 out of the 31 possible trimers, tetramers, and pentamers searched were found in C. difficile.
source: 25 out of the 31 possible trimers, tetramers, and pentamers searched were found (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a result from the C. difficile analysis.

claim: Comparison of biological replicates revealed a high reproducibility in C. difficile analysis, both in retention times and quantification.
source: Comparison of biological replicates revealed a high reproducibility, both in retention times and quantification.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment of data quality.

claim: A high correlation was found between biological replicates in C. difficile analysis, confirming the robustness of the quantification method.
source: A high correlation was found between biological replicates, confirming the robustness of the quantification method (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Both C. difficile strains R20291 and M7404 contained a similar amount of mono-, tri-, tetra-, and pentamers.
source: Both strains contained a similar amount of mono-, tri-, tetra-, and pentamers, but strain M7404 contained a significantly lower proportion of monomers and a higher proportion of dimers than strain R20291 (p=0.022 and p=0.005, respectively; Student's t-test; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a comparative result shown in Figure 4b.

claim: C. difficile strain M7404 contained a significantly lower proportion of monomers than strain R20291 (p=0.022).
source: Both strains contained a similar amount of mono-, tri-, tetra-, and pentamers, but strain M7404 contained a significantly lower proportion of monomers and a higher proportion of dimers than strain R20291 (p=0.022 and p=0.005, respectively; Student's t-test; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a statistically significant result shown in Figure 4b.

claim: C. difficile strain M7404 contained a significantly higher proportion of dimers than strain R20291 (p=0.005).
source: Both strains contained a similar amount of mono-, tri-, tetra-, and pentamers, but strain M7404 contained a significantly lower proportion of monomers and a higher proportion of dimers than strain R20291 (p=0.022 and p=0.005, respectively; Student's t-test; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a statistically significant result shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Two muropeptides (Lac-AEJ[AG] and Lac-AEJ-Lac-AEJA) were significantly less abundant in C. difficile strain R20291 compared to M7404.
source: Two muropeptides were significantly less abundant (Lac-AEJ[AG] and Lac-AEJ-Lac-AEJA), and four others were significantly more abundant in strain R20291 (Lac-AEJV- Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJ[L/I]-Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJAA-Lac-AEJA and the trimer (Lac-AEJA)3).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Four muropeptides (Lac-AEJV-Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJ[L/I]-Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJAA-Lac-AEJA and the trimer (Lac-AEJA)3) were significantly more abundant in C. difficile strain R20291 compared to M7404.
source: Two muropeptides were significantly less abundant (Lac-AEJ[AG] and Lac-AEJ-Lac-AEJA), and four others were significantly more abundant in strain R20291 (Lac-AEJV- Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJ[L/I]-Lac-AEJA, Lac-AEJAA-Lac-AEJA and the trimer (Lac-AEJA)3).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The differences in muropeptide abundance between C. difficile strains are likely to reflect different substrate specificities for PBPs and the Ddl ligases in these strains.
source: These differences are likely to reflect different substrate specificities for PBPs and the Ddl ligases in these strains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative results.

claim: Combining the output of PGFinder with statistical analysis of muropeptide abundance offers a robust workflow to identify differences in PG composition.
source: Therefore, combining the output of PGFinder with statistical analysis of muropeptide abundance offers a robust workflow to identify differences in PG composition.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the C. difficile comparative analysis.

claim: PGFinder identified 63 muropeptides out of the 71 reported by Anderson et al. for P. aeruginosa.
source: PGFinder identified 63 muropeptides out of the 71 reported by Anderson et al., matching our search criteria (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from benchmarking against published data.

claim: The eight muropeptides that were not identified in P. aeruginosa were absent from the list of deconvoluted masses.
source: The eight muropeptides that were not identified were absent from the list of deconvoluted masses, indicating that the problem was not associated with the script, highlighting that the deconvolution step is a source of variability.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for missing identifications.

claim: The deconvolution step is a source of variability in PG analysis.
source: The eight muropeptides that were not identified were absent from the list of deconvoluted masses, indicating that the problem was not associated with the script, highlighting that the deconvolution step is a source of variability.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the benchmarking analysis.

claim: The observed masses calculated using Byos Feature Finder were closer to the theoretical value (6.5 ppm versus 10.7 ppm on average) for P. aeruginosa.
source: Interestingly, the observed masses calculated using Byos Feature Finder were closer to the theoretical value (6.5 ppm versus 10.7 ppm on average), reflecting another source of variability associated with data deconvolution.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of deconvolution accuracy.

claim: Four muropeptides previously identified containing the AEJAG pentapeptide stem were matched with distinct structures due to a mass coincidence between K and AG.
source: Four muropeptides previously identified containing the AEJAG pentapeptide stem were matched with distinct structures due to a mass coincidence between K and AG.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the P. aeruginosa analysis.

claim: MS/MS spectra analysis suggested that muropeptides contained a K residue rather than the AG dipeptide.
source: A careful analysis of MS/MS spectra suggested that these muropeptides contained a K residue rather than the AG dipeptide (the y2 ion being 143 ppm away from the expected mass), showing the added value of an unbiased search.
evidence: This is stated as a result from MS/MS validation.

claim: The tetrapeptide AEJK elutes before EAJA whilst the pentapeptide AEJAG elutes later in the chromatography.
source: This conclusion is supported by the retention times of the corresponding muropeptides since the tetrapeptide AEJK elutes before EAJA whilst the pentapeptide AEJAG elutes later in the chromatography (Bern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as evidence for the structural assignment.

claim: The PGFinder search identified a large number of muropeptides in P. aeruginosa that were not reported previously.
source: It is worth noting that our search also identified a large number of muropeptides that were not reported previously (Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as an additional finding from the P. aeruginosa analysis.

claim: The PG analysis pipeline can identify an unprecedentedly large number of muropeptide structures based on MS1 data.
source: These results collectively show that our PG analysis pipeline can identify an unprecedentedly large number of muropeptide structures based on MS1 data, including all those previously reported (Anderson et al., 2020a; Anderson et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the benchmarking analysis.

claim: MaxQuant was selected as a free alternative software for mass deconvolution.
source: We sought to identify a free alternative software for mass deconvolution to make our PG analysis pipeline accessible to everyone. MaxQuant was selected as a tool of choice since it represents a widely used software package to analyse high-resolution mass-spectrometric data for shotgun proteomics (Cox and Mann, 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: MaxQuant has native support for Thermo MS data (RAW) and Sciex (WIFF) file formats and supports the open MS data format mzXML.
source: MaxQuant has native support for Thermo MS data (RAW) and Sciex (WIFF) file formats and supports the open MS data format mzXML.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of MaxQuant.

claim: Virtually any proprietary MS data file can be converted to the mzXML open format using freely available tools such as Proteowizard and TOPPAS.
source: Virtually any proprietary MS data file can be converted to the mzXML open format using freely available tools such as Proteowizard and TOPPAS, making this workflow universally applicable.
evidence: This is stated as a capability that makes the workflow accessible.

claim: All expected muropeptides were identified in P. aeruginosa data processed using MaxQuant and PGFinder.
source: We were able to identify all the expected muropeptides (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the MaxQuant validation.

claim: The automated analysis of PG datasets can be carried out using the MaxQuant freeware and PGFinder.
source: This result confirms that the automated analysis of PG datasets can be carried out using the MaxQuant freeware and our open-source script PGFinder (Table 2 and Table 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MaxQuant validation.

claim: MS analysis of bacterial PG has been carried out since the late 1980s.
source: MS analysis of bacterial PG has been carried out since the late 1980s (Garcia-Bustos et al., 1988; Martin et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Data analysis for PG MS remains a manual process.
source: Whilst rp-HPLC-MS is now routinely used to explore PG structure, data analysis remains a manual process.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the field.

claim: Manual data analysis has become a bottleneck that prevents high-throughput analyses and introduces issues regarding reproducibility.
